claims.text: The starting material is a homogeneous equiatomic solid solution of Nb, Ta, Zr, Hf, and Ti.
Arc melting or comparable standard synthesis techniques can produce the specified homogeneous solid solution.
Each of the five elements is present at approximately 20 atomic percent and therefore above the 5 atomic percent threshold.
Hydrostatic pressure up to 20 GPa modifies the alloy's lattice parameters.
Hydrostatic pressure modifies the alloy's phonon spectrum and vibrational dynamics.
Pressure generally reduces the lattice parameters of the alloy.
Changes in lattice parameters alter the alloy's phonon modes and vibrational spectrum.
Changes in lattice vibrational dynamics modify the density of phonon states relevant to electron pairing.
The pressure-induced phonon changes alter the electron–phonon coupling strength.
Electron–phonon coupling strength governs the superconducting transition temperature of the specified alloy.
The alloy has a measurable superconducting transition and gap features at ambient pressure.
The superconducting transition temperature will evolve systematically with applied pressure relative to its ambient-pressure value.
The pressure dependence of the transition temperature may show an initial increase followed by saturation or decline as the lattice stiffens.
Changes in superconducting transition temperature should correlate with pressure-induced changes in lattice constants.
Excessive lattice stiffening can weaken the superconducting response or cause the transition temperature to saturate.
The proposed mechanism is applicable only while the material remains a single solid-solution phase without significant segregation or a structural phase transition.
A lack of correlation between pressure-induced lattice or phonon changes and transition-temperature shifts would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
Transition-temperature changes occurring only upon a structural phase transition would falsify the proposed single-phase lattice-tuning mechanism.
